title: Why Scale Is The Real Moat In Ad Auctions
documentTitle: Microsoft 'Baja' Financial Model Presentation to Apple — October 2018
excerptForBlog:
Scale evidence: Impact from original Yahoo supply

Key Takeaways: We have empirical proof from our Yahoo! Search deal that incremental volume drives up RPMs. With the influx of Yahoo! Traffic into our ecosystem in 2012 we were able to realize a one-time boost to our RPMs driven by injection of scale. In addition, having a bigger marketplace enabled us to increase our innovation which had driven up our RPMs even further over the next couple years.

We believe that injection of Apple volume would enable us to realize RPM lifts from scale and innovation similar to the Yahoo! deal. We would expect that these lifts would help us get to [redacted] of Google on iPad and Mac in the US. In international markets we would be able to get to [redacted] of Google on iPhone.

Notes: RPM increases with scale as advertisers increase bids to be on top in the auction, and algorithms improve with more data. The curve is initially steep as small increases in scale meaningfully improve advertiser participation, making it possible to offset fixed cost of investing in another platform. Product innovation shifts performance to a higher RPM curve, not along the same curve. Most of subsequent performance improvements come from innovation and demand expansion.

lessonTitle: Why Scale Is The Real Moat In Ad Auctions
pullQuote: In ad markets, scale isn't just an advantage — it's the price of admission to compete at all.
situation: In October 2018, Microsoft's Kate Plikus presented a financial model to Apple, internally codenamed 'Baja,' arguing that Apple should make Bing its default search engine. The pitch rested on a single core claim: Microsoft had already proven, via its 2012 Yahoo deal, that a sudden jump in search volume produced lasting revenue gains. The document surfaced as a trial exhibit in the U.S. Department of Justice antitrust case against Google.
insight: The slide draws a sharp distinction most founders miss. The document says 'product innovation shifts performance to a higher RPM curve, not along the same curve.' That's the hidden insight. Scale doesn't just improve your existing system incrementally — at some threshold, it justifies new investment, which permanently re-floors your performance. Microsoft is saying: the Yahoo traffic injection in 2012 didn't just add queries, it funded improvements that kept paying off 'over the next couple years.' This is a network-effects compounding argument — more data improves the auction algorithm, better algorithms attract more advertisers, higher bids raise RPMs. The pitch to Apple is essentially: your volume is the unlock. We can't get to that new curve without you, and once we're there, the economics work for both of us. The redacted RPM targets (described as percentages 'of Google') hint at how significant the gap still was, but context on those specific numbers is not available from this document.
application: If you're pitching a partnership, don't just show revenue share projections. Show the partner what threshold effect their volume creates — what new capability, investment, or competitive position becomes possible only at their scale. Frame it as a curve jump, not a line extension. That's a fundamentally stronger argument.
